q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR AS I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY) > 100 AND MAX(I.SALARY) < 75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR AS I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY) >= 100 AND MAX(I.SALARY) < 75

counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUDGET) VALUES ('History', 100000); INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (1, 'John Doe', 50, 'History'), (2, 'Jane Smith', 50, 'History');
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the HAVING clause condition for the sum of instructor salaries. Q1 uses '>', while Q2 uses '>='. This difference can lead to different results if the sum of salaries is exactly 100.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have a department with a total salary of exactly 100. In this case, Q1 will not include this department in the result, but Q2 will.
